title: Turkey: Istanbul 'lion hunt' ends with no big cat found after all
summary: After a major search operation for a "loose lion" in Istanbul woodlands, Turkish authorities said "the animal was neither a lion nor any other big cat."

image.caption: Prosecutors in Istanbul said an investigation was underway to establish who owned the animal [FILE: January 14, 2026]Image: Tokyo Zoological Park Society/REUTERS

blocks.text: A large-scale search operation by Turkish authorities in woodland north of Istanbul revealed that the animal was neither a lion nor any other type of big cat, according to the Istanbul governor's office.

The governor's office first issued a statement on Sunday evening saying that security cameras had captured footage of a "loose lion" in Sariyer, north of Istanbul's European side. It said "the lion has been located and the efforts to capture it were underway."
The parks authority also said in an online statement that police officers in the area had spotted "an animal resembling a lion" on surveillance cameras.
Turkish media published grainy images of "a lioness walking through a grassy area." Some media reports suggested "it had escaped from a nearby home."
Then a major search operation went underway. Specialist veterinarians joined the efforts to capture the animal, park authorities said.

blocks.caption: Turkish media published thermal images of a "lioness roaming free"Image: Anka

blocks.text: Even the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office issued a statement saying it launched an investigation focused on identifying the lions owner.
After a day of search however, the Istanbul governor's office said "no ​concrete evidence indicating ‌the presence of a lion was found."
It said ⁠"based on new footage, it has been determined ⁠that the ​animal in the footage is neither a lion nor any other species of big cat."
The governor's office did not provide further information about what the animal seen in the footage was.
The authorities said this was not a case of a loose lion but it sparked an outrage among activists and advocates.
Northern Forests Defense, an independent ecology advocacy movement, called for "the individuals who illegally held this lion captive to be identified and brought to justice."
"Removing wild animals from their natural habitats and keeping them in captivity in villas is a crime," the organization said on X.
Wildlife conservationist Gokce Coskun said on X that "there are thousands of people keeping lions illegally in Turkey" and "licensed 'lion parks' have sprung up everywhere."
Last year, a lion that escaped from a "theme park" near the southern city of Antalya was shot dead after attacking a man.

Doganay Tolunay, an ecology professor at Istanbul University, said questions must be raised about how a globally threatened species was brought into Turkey, how it passed through customs and why those keeping it have not been identified.
Although keeping wild animals as pets are forbidden in Turkey, it has become a hub for the illegal trade in wild animals as traffickers exploit its air links to Africa and Asia.
In December 2024, a young gorilla was rescued after being discovered at Istanbul Airport on a flight from Nigeria to Thailand.
